---
title: "Stress-Constrained Truss Optimization"
toc: true
---

## Description

This tutorial demonstrates stress-constrained truss optimization on the classic
10-bar truss benchmark (Haftka & Gürdal). We first compute the axial stress in
every member with [`TrussStressFun`](../reference/), then optimize twice:

- **Compliance-only**: minimize compliance under a volume-fraction constraint.
- **Fully-stressed design (FSD)**: minimize the volume subject to a limit on
  every member's axial stress, using the ε-relaxed stress constraints of
  Cheng & Guo (1997).

Stress-constrained truss optimization is genuinely harder than compliance
minimization because of the **stress singularity problem** (Sved & Ginos,
1968): the optimum often requires removing a member, but the member's stress
constraint is violated throughout the removal path, so a plain
gradient-based optimizer cannot reach it. ε-relaxation replaces
`g_e = |σ_e|/σ_lim − 1 ≤ 0` with `g_e = x_e (|σ_e|/σ_lim − 1) − ε ≤ 0`:
at `x_e = 0` the constraint becomes `−ε ≤ 0`, which opens the degenerate
subspaces. The resulting FSD design trades stiffness for weight: its members
carry stresses near the limit.

## Setup

```{julia}
#| output: false
using TopOpt, LinearAlgebra
using StaticArrays: SVector
using WGLMakie
WGLMakie.activate!(; resize_to=:parent)
using Bonito
if haskey(ENV, "QUARTO_PROJECT_DIR")
    Bonito.Page(exportable=true, offline=true)
else
    Bonito.browser_display()
end
display_app(app) = display(app)
```

## Define the 10-bar truss

The 10-bar truss has 6 nodes and 10 members: two bottom-edge nodes loaded
downward, the bottom-left corner pinned, and the bottom-right corner on a
roller. Each member's design variable scales its cross-sectional area.

```{julia}
#| output: false
node_points = Dict(
    1 => SVector(0.0, 0.0), 2 => SVector(360.0, 0.0), 3 => SVector(720.0, 0.0),
    4 => SVector(720.0, 360.0), 5 => SVector(360.0, 360.0), 6 => SVector(0.0, 360.0),
)
elements = Dict(
    1 => (5, 3), 2 => (1, 3), 3 => (4, 1), 4 => (5, 4), 5 => (3, 2),
    6 => (1, 2), 7 => (4, 2), 8 => (3, 4), 9 => (2, 5), 10 => (1, 5),
)
mats = TrussFEAMaterial(1.0, 0.3)
crosssecs = TrussFEACrossSec(1.0)
fixities = Dict(1 => SVector(true, true), 3 => SVector(false, true))
loads = Dict(2 => SVector(0.0, -1.0), 4 => SVector(0.0, -1.0))
problem = TrussProblem(node_points, elements, loads, fixities, mats, crosssecs)
ncells = length(elements)
```

## Compute the member stresses

[`TrussStressFun`](../reference/) computes the axial stress in each member from
the nodal displacements and the penalized design. Compressive stress is
negative, tensile stress is positive. We solve the full design first:

```{julia}
#| output: false
solver = FEASolver(DirectSolver, problem; xmin=0.0001)
ts = TrussStressFun(solver)
vol = VolumeFun(solver; fraction=true)
comp = ComplianceFun(solver)
```

```{julia}
#| output: true
xfull = ones(ncells)
σfull = ts(PseudoDensities(xfull))
println("full design: peak |σ| = $(round(maximum(abs, σfull), digits=4))")
println("member stresses: ", round.(σfull; digits=3))
```

The peak stress of the full design is the reference value for choosing the
stress limit below.

## Compliance-only optimization

Minimize compliance subject to a 50% volume fraction:

```{julia}
#| output: true
obj(x) = comp(PseudoDensities(x))
m1 = Model(obj)
addvar!(m1, zeros(ncells), fill(3.0, ncells))
Nonconvex.add_ineq_constraint!(m1, x -> vol(PseudoDensities(x)) - 0.5)
r1 = Nonconvex.optimize(
    m1, MMA87(), fill(0.5, ncells);
    options=MMAOptions(; maxiter=200, tol=Nonconvex.Tolerance(; kkt=1e-3, f=1e-3))
)
x1 = r1.minimizer
σ1 = ts(PseudoDensities(x1))
println("compliance-only: compliance = $(round(obj(x1), digits=3)), ")
println("  volume = $(round(vol(PseudoDensities(x1)), digits=3)), peak |σ| = $(round(maximum(abs, σ1), digits=3))")
```

The compliance-only design concentrates area in the stiffest load paths; its
peak stress (per unit area) is the value a stress constraint must cut below.

## Stress-constrained (fully-stressed) design

Minimize the volume subject to ε-relaxed stress constraints
`x_e (|σ_e|/σ_lim − 1) − ε ≤ 0`, starting from the full design. `σ_lim` is set
below the full design's peak so the constraints are active, and `ε` relaxes
them near zero area so members can be removed:

```{julia}
#| output: true
σlim = 0.9 * maximum(abs, σfull)
ε = 0.02
g(x) = epsilon_relaxed(abs.(ts(PseudoDensities(x))), x, σlim, ε)
m2 = Model(x -> vol(PseudoDensities(x)))
addvar!(m2, zeros(ncells), fill(3.0, ncells))
Nonconvex.add_ineq_constraint!(m2, g)
r2 = Nonconvex.optimize(
    m2, MMA87(), copy(xfull);
    options=MMAOptions(; maxiter=300, tol=Nonconvex.Tolerance(; kkt=1e-3, f=1e-3))
)
x2 = r2.minimizer
σ2 = ts(PseudoDensities(x2))
println("stress-constrained: volume = $(round(vol(PseudoDensities(x2)), digits=3)), ")
println("  compliance = $(round(comp(PseudoDensities(x2)), digits=3)), peak |σ| = $(round(maximum(abs, σ2), digits=3))")
println("  (σ_lim = $(round(σlim, digits=4)))")
```

The stress-constrained design is lighter than the compliance-only design at
the same time as its active members carry stresses near `σ_lim`. The reported
peak can exceed `σ_lim` slightly: the ε-relaxed constraint allows a slack of
`ε/x_e` per member, which is the price of keeping the removal path open.

## Visualize the designs

Member area (line width) and axial stress (color) of the two designs:

```{julia}
#| label: fig-trs-stress
#| fig-cap: "Stress-constrained truss design: member areas and axial stresses"
app = visualize(
    problem;
    static=true,
    topology=x2,
    cell_colors=σ2,
    draw_legend=true,
)
display_app(app)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-trs-comp
#| fig-cap: "Compliance-only truss design for comparison"
app = visualize(
    problem;
    static=true,
    topology=x1,
    cell_colors=σ1,
    draw_legend=true,
)
display_app(app)
```

## References

- Sved, G., & Ginos, Z. (1968). *Structural optimization under multiple
  loading.* International Journal of Mechanical Sciences.
- Cheng, G. D., & Guo, X. (1997). *ε-relaxed approach in structural topology
  optimization.* Structural Optimization.
- Haftka, R. T., & Gürdal, Z. (1992). *Elements of Structural Optimization.*
  Kluwer Academic Publishers.
